kurz: Graham's rule-of-thumb growth formula, his price ceiling and his asset-based value from the balance sheet are three valuation methods, of which only the growth formula needs a forecast.

bloecke.md:
Benjamin Graham's rules are the oldest valuation methods still in use today. He devised a rule-of-thumb formula for growing companies, a price ceiling built from two multiples and an asset-based value calculated from the balance sheet alone. The price ceiling and the asset-based value manage entirely without a forecast of the future, while the rule-of-thumb formula needs an estimate of future growth.

None of the three methods estimates an intrinsic value. They draw a line, either a price above which you should not buy or a value below which the share price should not fall. That is less than a discounted cash flow promises, but it holds up longer, because you can observe whether a line has been crossed. With a point estimate this is not possible.

## Graham's growth formula

In 1962 Graham presented a short formula that can be used to check what growth a share price implies. In 1974 he added an interest rate factor, because a share is always valued in comparison with the bond as the alternative.

bloecke.erklaerung: The value per share results from current earnings, a base P/E for zero growth and a linear premium for growth. The factor 4.4 / Y raises or lowers the result when the level of interest rates differs from that of 1962.
variablen: earnings per share over the last twelve months
expected annual earnings growth over the next seven to ten years, in percentage points
price-to-earnings ratio of a company with no growth
yield on top-rated corporate bonds in 1962, as a percentage
today's yield on top-rated corporate bonds, as a percentage

bloecke.md: Y requires a current value. Ten-year German federal bonds (Bunds) yielded 3.52% on 18 September 2026. The spread for top-rated corporate bonds was recently around 0.4 percentage points, which together gives around 3.9%. The correction factor 4.4 / 3.9 is therefore around 1.13. The 1974 version thus currently gives values about 13% higher than the original version.

bloecke.titel: Permissible P/E under the Graham formula for each growth rate
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. Because the formula is linear in g, every additional percentage point of growth raises the permissible P/E by exactly two points, or by about 2.26 points in the 1974 version at Y = 3.9%, regardless of how long the growth lasts.

bloecke.md: The chart shows the weakness of the formula. With expected growth of just over 3%, and in the interest rate version with just under two and a half per cent, the formula already allows a P/E above 15. That is above the limit Graham sets for defensive investors in the same book. At 20% growth, the P/E comes to 49 and 55 respectively. The formula does not take into account how long growth lasts, how much capital it ties up and what comes afterwards. A discounted cash flow with a declining growth rate reflects these three points. That is why the formula is not suitable as a valuation. Its purpose is to translate a share price into an implied growth rate.

Graham expressly did not recommend using the formula. It values growth companies with a systematic bias, because growth enters the calculation linearly and without any time limit. Only the reverse use makes sense. You enter the share price and earnings, solve for g and check whether the implied growth is plausible. From €4.00 of earnings and a share price of €100, with Y = 3.9, the result is a g of around 6.8, sustained for ten years. This assumption can be checked; the value of €83.49 cannot.

## The Graham number

The second building block is the product of two ceilings. Graham allowed the defensive investor a P/E of at most 15, calculated on average earnings over the last three years and not on a single year. In addition there was a price-to-book ratio of at most 1.5. He allowed a higher price-to-book ratio with a correspondingly lower P/E, as long as the product of the two is at most 22.5. Rearranging this exception rule gives a maximum price.

bloecke.formel: Maximum price = sqrt(22.5 × earnings per share × book value per share)
bloecke.erklaerung: The factor 22.5 is the product 15 × 1.5. The expression is the geometric mean of the price limit based on earnings and the price limit based on assets.
bloecke.beispiel: Earnings per share €5.00, book value per share €30.00:  sqrt(22.5 × 5 × 30) = sqrt(3,375) = €58.09. At a share price of €72, the P/E of 14.4 would be acceptable, but the P/B would be 2.4. The product of 34.6 exceeds the limit.

bloecke.md: Today the criterion excludes almost every high-quality company. The reason lies in the accounting rules and not in prices. Internally generated brands, customer lists and publishing rights may not be capitalised under Section 248(2) HGB (Commercial Code). IAS 38 prohibits capitalising the same items, and research costs are expensed immediately under IAS 38 as under the HGB. Development costs, for example for internally developed software, may be capitalised at the company's option under the HGB. Under IAS 38 they must be capitalised as soon as strict evidence of feasibility and future benefit is available. Companies that put their capital into software, formulations and brand building therefore usually have little book value. Share buybacks reinforce the effect, because they reduce equity and mathematically increase the P/B. Graham's limit of 1.5 dates from a time when companies consisted mainly of factories, warehouses and machinery.

bloecke.md:
## Net current asset value

The strictest method ignores earnings altogether. Net current asset value (NCAV) starts from [[Current assets|current assets]] and deducts all liabilities and provisions from them, including long-term ones. Fixed assets are set at zero. Graham systematically bought only when the share price was below two thirds of this value. The difference is the [[Margin of safety|margin of safety]] in the literal sense.

bloecke.unter: Model balance sheet of a small public limited company (AG) in € million. Property, plant and equipment with a book value of €60 million does not enter the calculation.

bloecke.md:
The model company's NCAV is €38.0 million. With 5.0 million shares, that is €7.60 per share, and two thirds of that is €5.07. If the share trades at €4.60 (market value €23.0 million), the condition is met.

Looked at another way, a buyer of all the shares pays €23 million for the entire company. In return, the buyer receives short-term assets with a book value of €105 million, against which there are €67 million of debts. Mathematically, the buyer gets machinery, buildings and land with a book value of €60 million thrown in at no extra cost.

What remains open is whether the balance sheet values hold up if it comes to the worst. For this test, Graham applied rough discounts in *Security Analysis*: cash at full value, receivables at a discount, inventories at a substantial discount and property, plant and equipment at an almost token value. If you work through the model balance sheet with these assumptions, the estimated liquidation value is below the NCAV. The NCAV is therefore not always the more conservative figure.

bloecke.titel: Model balance sheet with Graham's liquidation discounts

bloecke.md:
## The decline of net-nets

There are three reasons why the search for net-nets hardly produces any hits today.

First, balance sheets today contain less asset backing. A software company has no inventories, and a service provider has hardly any receivables that could support a market value. Structurally, the method only works for capital-intensive businesses, that is, where earning power is also weak.

Second, markets are searched systematically today. Balance sheet data is available free of charge, and screeners deliver results in seconds. What Graham found by laboriously leafing through manuals, all market participants now find at the same time. The gap therefore closes faster or not at all.

Third, there is usually a reason for the remaining cases. A company that trades permanently below its NCAV is usually losing money continuously, depends on one major customer or is run by a majority shareholder who disregards the interests of minority shareholders.

The NCAV applies only at the balance sheet date. If the model company loses €6 million a year, the NCAV falls from 38 to 32, then to 26 and then to €20 million. After two and a half years it has fallen to the €23 million market value at the time of purchase. The margin of safety is then used up, even though the share price has not moved. Without a trigger that closes the gap (sale, distribution, capital reduction, takeover), the success of the position depends on the share price approaching the NCAV faster than the NCAV falls.

A German peculiarity shifts the figure further. Under Section 253(2) HGB, pension provisions are discounted at the ten-year average of the market interest rate. In a period of rising interest rates, the provision is therefore more likely to be set too high, and in a period of falling rates too low. The deduction in the NCAV is thus less reliable than it looks.

bloecke.titel: Valuation of current assets under the HGB
bloecke.md: German accounting law is geared towards protecting creditors. Acquisition cost forms the upper limit of value, and current assets are subject to the strict lower of cost or market principle (strenges Niederstwertprinzip, Section 253(4) HGB). Inventories and receivables must be written down as soon as their market value is below book value, and may never be written up above acquisition cost. Current assets under the HGB are therefore, if in doubt, more likely to be stated too low than too high, which suits the method. This does not apply in the same way to IFRS financial statements with fair value accounting.

## Return on the cigar butt approach

Buffett compared this approach to a discarded cigar butt that still offers one free puff. What is meant is an abandoned business that is bought far below its asset value, held until the gap closes and then sold. Why Buffett later gave up the method can be shown by calculation. If the share price rises from two thirds of the NCAV to the full NCAV, the gain is always 50%. How high the resulting annual return turns out to be depends solely on the waiting time.

bloecke.titel: Annual return from a 50% price gain by holding period
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation (1.5 to the power of 1/n minus 1). The annual return on an asset-based purchase depends almost entirely on when the market closes the gap, and this point in time cannot be predicted.

bloecke.md: From a waiting time of about five and a half years, the asset-based purchase returns less than a broad world equity index. In addition, the return ends with the sale, and the next idea is needed for the money straight away. A business that permanently earns 12% on retained earnings needs neither a second idea nor a buyer. This is the basis of Buffett's remark in his 1989 shareholder letter that it is far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Buffett added that Munger had understood this early on. There is also the problem of scale. Net-nets are by nature very small, so a large portfolio cannot build a position of meaningful size in them.

bloecke.titel: Tax cost of turning over the portfolio
bloecke.md:
Realised price gains are subject to 25% [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] and a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on top of that, 26.375% in total (Section 32d(1) EStG, Income Tax Act), plus church tax where applicable. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG) is quickly used up with larger amounts.

Suppose two strategies each earn 10% a year before tax over 15 years:

- With a single sale at the end, €1 first becomes €4.18. After tax on the gain, €3.34 remains, which corresponds to 8.4% a year after tax.
- With a sale every three years, each cycle brings 33.1%, of which 24.4% remains after tax. After five cycles the final value is €2.98, that is 7.5% a year.

The difference of just over 0.8 percentage points a year arises solely from deferring the tax. Investors who constantly turn over their portfolio pay this price permanently. The asset-based method forces a sale as soon as the discount has disappeared.

- A basket makes more sense than a single share. Graham held dozens of such positions at the same time. The method is statistical in design: individual holdings fall to zero, and the result comes from the average. A single position therefore does not reproduce the method on a small scale, because the balancing out across many holdings is missing.
- A special rule applies to loss offsetting. Losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG), and the bank keeps a separate share loss pot (Aktien-Verlusttopf) for this. A basket in which some holdings fail generates losses in this pot that cannot be offset against interest or gains on funds.
- The figures come from the annual financial statements that German incorporated companies must disclose in the Company Register (Unternehmensregister) under Section 325 HGB. For shares traded on the open market (Freiverkehr), this is often the only reliable source, and the figures are several months old. For a method based on snapshots, this is a considerable weakness.
- Tradability should be checked before buying. For the shares of very small companies, the bid-ask spread sometimes costs more than a year's expected return.

Graham's methods provide limits but not company values. The Graham number indicates the price above which you should no longer buy. The NCAV indicates what is left of current assets at book values after deducting all debts. Neither says anything about the quality of the business. That is why they only work in a basket and only for capital-intensive companies.

bloecke.titel: Interest rate factor in the 1974 version
bloecke.md: The factor 4.4 / Y is the only part of the formula that has carried over into modern valuation practice. There it is called the discount rate. A share is always valued in comparison with the low-risk alternative. If the bond yield rises, the present value of the same future payments falls. In 1962 Y was 4.4%; today it is around 3.9%, so the factor has a slightly increasing effect. In the high interest rate period of the early 1980s, with double-digit bond yields, it would have more than halved the values. The formula without this factor implicitly assumes the 1962 level of interest rates.

mitnehmen: The Graham formula is linear in growth and therefore unsuitable as a valuation; only the reverse is useful, deriving the implied growth from a share price.

The Graham number is the geometric mean of the price limits from a P/E of 15 and a P/B of 1.5 and today excludes almost everything, mainly because internally generated brands and customer lists may not be recognised on the balance sheet and research costs are expensed immediately.
The NCAV deducts all liabilities from current assets and sets fixed assets at zero; buying only takes place below two thirds of this value.
The discount only helps if it closes, and at a waiting time of eight years a 50% gain already corresponds to only 5.2% a year, which is less than a broad index has delivered historically.
Asset-based methods force sales and therefore ongoing taxation; the tax deferral from holding a company for the long term is a separate, calculable advantage.

begriffe.text: Price ceiling for defensive investors, calculated as the square root of (22.5 × earnings per share × book value per share). The factor 22.5 is the product of the limits P/E 15 and P/B 1.5.
Current assets less all liabilities and provisions, with fixed assets set at zero. Graham only bought below two thirds of this value.
Buying an economically abandoned company far below its asset value in order to take one last profit. The approach only works with small sums and forces constant selling.
Current assets divided by current liabilities. Graham required a value of at least 2.0 for the defensive investor; for business models with advance payment, a lower value is normal.
